guide.title: Your first API requests
guide.subtitle: A friendly guide to ReqDeck for people who have never sent a request.
guide.practice: A free public API that answers whatever you send. Safe to experiment on.
shortcuts: Explain what is under the pointer or in the field you type in.
Find a request or a command.
Rename the selected item in the tree.
Close the help or a dialog.

start.title: Getting started
start.what: ReqDeck sends requests to web services (APIs) and shows what they answer.
start.why: You can try an API without writing code, and keep the requests you need.
start.example: Open Samples on the start screen, open the folder JSONPlaceholder, pick "Get a post", and press Send.
start.next: Point at any field or button and press F1 to learn what it does.

menu.title: Menu
menu.what: All commands of ReqDeck, grouped by what they work on.
menu.why: Commands you do not see as buttons are here, with their shortcuts.
menu.example: File > Import cURL turns a copied command into a request.
menu.next: Most commands also have a shortcut, shown next to them.

topbar.environment.title: Environment
topbar.environment.what: Chooses which set of variables your requests use right now.
topbar.environment.why: The same requests can go to a test server or to the real one without changes.
topbar.environment.example: Switch from "Staging" to "Production", and {{baseUrl}} points to the other server.
topbar.environment.next: Use the button next to it to create or edit environments.

topbar.manageEnvironments.title: Manage environments
topbar.manageEnvironments.what: Opens the list of environments and their variables.
topbar.manageEnvironments.why: Here you define values such as addresses and keys once, for all requests.
topbar.manageEnvironments.example: Add a variable baseUrl with the value https://httpbin.org.
topbar.manageEnvironments.next: Then write {{baseUrl}}/get in the URL of a request.

topbar.save.title: Save workspace
topbar.save.what: Writes all requests and environments to the workspace file.
topbar.save.why: Changes live only in memory until you save them.
topbar.save.example: Press Ctrl+S after editing a request.
topbar.save.next: The status bar shows when the workspace has unsaved changes.

topbar.settings.title: Settings
topbar.settings.what: Opens the settings of the application.
topbar.settings.why: Here you choose the language, the folder for new workspaces, and update checks.
topbar.settings.example: Pick the folder where new workspaces are created.

collection.tree.title: Collection
collection.tree.what: Your saved requests, sorted into folders.
collection.tree.why: You do not have to type a request again: click it and send it.
collection.tree.example: Right-click to add a request or a folder, rename, duplicate, or delete.
collection.tree.next: Ctrl+click or Shift+click selects several items for Delete or Duplicate. With the keyboard: arrows move and open folders, F2 renames, Delete deletes. Right-click > Sort A–Z puts folders first, then sorts by name.

sidebar.tabs.title: Collection and History
sidebar.tabs.what: Switches the left pane between your saved requests and the requests you sent.
sidebar.tabs.why: History lets you find a request you sent earlier, even if you never saved it.
sidebar.tabs.example: Open History to see the last requests with their status.
sidebar.tabs.next: Double-click an entry in History to make a request from it.

history.list.title: History
history.list.what: The requests you sent, newest first, with their status and time.
history.list.why: You can repeat or inspect what you did before.
history.list.example: Green 200 means success, orange 404 means "not found", red means a failure.
history.list.next: Double-click an entry, or select it and press Return, to make a request from it. Passwords are not kept.

history.clear.title: Clear history
history.clear.what: Removes all entries from the history.
history.clear.why: Useful when the list gets long or holds requests you do not need.
history.clear.example: ReqDeck asks before it removes anything.
history.clear.next: Your saved requests are not affected.

request.name.title: Request name
request.name.what: The name under which the request appears in the collection.
request.name.why: A clear name helps you find the request later.
request.name.next: Click the name to change it; it is stored when you leave the field.

request.method.title: Method
request.method.what: What the request asks the server to do.
request.method.why: The same address can mean different actions depending on the method.
request.method.example: GET reads, POST creates, PUT or PATCH changes, DELETE removes.
request.method.next: Most APIs say in their documentation which method to use.

request.url.title: Address (URL)
request.url.what: Where the request goes, like the address of a website in a browser.
request.url.why: It names the server and the thing you want from it.
request.url.next: Press Send or Ctrl+Enter. A red, underlined {{name}} is a variable without a value.

request.send.title: Send
request.send.what: Sends the request and waits for the answer.
request.send.why: The answer appears on the right: status, time, size, and content.
request.send.example: Press Ctrl+Enter from any field of the request.
request.send.next: While the request runs, the button cancels it.

request.tabs.title: Parts of a request
request.tabs.what: Params, Headers, Body, and Auth are the parts a request can carry besides its address.
request.tabs.why: Each part answers a different question: what to filter, how to talk, what to send, who you are.
request.tabs.example: Add a parameter page=2 in Params to ask for the second page.
request.tabs.next: Many requests need only the URL; the other parts are optional.

request.params.title: Parameters
request.params.what: Name and value pairs added to the address after a question mark.
request.params.why: They tell the server what exactly you want, for example a search word or a page.
request.params.example: q = coffee becomes ?q=coffee at the end of the URL.
request.params.next: Clear the box at the start of a row to leave that parameter out for now.

request.headers.title: Headers
request.headers.what: Extra information sent with the request, as name and value pairs.
request.headers.why: Servers use headers to learn the format you send and accept, or who you are.
request.headers.example: Accept = application/json asks for an answer in JSON.
request.headers.next: For a login, use the Auth tab instead of typing the header by hand.

request.body.title: Body
request.body.what: Content sent with the request, usually when you create or change something.
request.body.why: POST, PUT, and PATCH requests often carry the new data here.
request.body.example: {"name": "Ann"} as JSON to create a user.
request.body.next: Choose the kind of body first; GET requests usually have none.

request.bodyMode.title: Kind of body
request.bodyMode.what: Chooses how the content is sent: none, raw text, or form fields.
request.bodyMode.why: The server expects one form, and the API documentation names it.
request.bodyMode.example: Raw with JSON for most modern APIs; Form for classic web forms.
request.bodyMode.next: The matching Content-Type header is added for you.

request.rawType.title: Format of the text
request.rawType.what: Says whether the raw text is JSON, XML, or plain text.
request.rawType.why: It sets the Content-Type header, so the server knows how to read the body.
request.rawType.next: Type the text in the field below.

request.rawBody.title: Body text
request.rawBody.what: The exact text sent as the body.
request.rawBody.why: Here you write the data the server should receive.
request.rawBody.next: Variables such as {{userId}} work here too.

request.form.title: Form fields
request.form.what: Name and value pairs sent like a web form.
request.form.why: Some servers expect data this way instead of JSON.
request.form.next: Clear the box at the start of a row to leave that field out.

request.authType.title: Authentication
request.authType.what: Chooses how the request proves who you are.
request.authType.why: Many APIs answer only to known users and refuse others with 401.
request.authType.example: Basic for a user name and password, Bearer for a token, API key for a key.
request.authType.next: The API documentation says which one it uses.

request.authUser.title: User name
request.authUser.what: The user name for Basic authentication.
request.authUser.why: Together with the password it identifies you to the server.
request.authUser.next: Prefer a variable for anything you would not show to others.

request.authPassword.title: Password
request.authPassword.why: It proves the user name belongs to you.
request.authPassword.example: {{password}}, with the value kept as a secret variable.
request.authPassword.next: A password typed here is stored in the workspace file; a secret variable is not.

request.token.title: Token
request.token.what: A key the server gave you, sent as "Bearer" with each request.
request.token.why: Many APIs use tokens instead of passwords.
request.token.example: {{token}}, with the value kept as a secret variable.
request.token.next: Tokens often expire; get a new one when the server answers 401.

request.apiKeyName.title: Key name
request.apiKeyName.what: The name under which the API key is sent.
request.apiKeyName.why: Each API chooses its own name for the key.
request.apiKeyName.next: Enter the key itself in the next field.

request.apiKeyValue.title: Key value
request.apiKeyValue.why: It identifies your account or app to the API.
request.apiKeyValue.example: {{apiKey}}, with the value kept as a secret variable.
request.apiKeyValue.next: Choose below whether it goes in a header or in the address.

request.apiKeyPlace.title: Where the key goes
request.apiKeyPlace.what: Chooses whether the key is sent as a header or as a parameter in the address.
request.apiKeyPlace.why: APIs expect it in one of the two places.
request.apiKeyPlace.example: Header is safer: addresses end up in logs more often.

request.timeout.title: Timeout
request.timeout.what: How long, in milliseconds, ReqDeck waits for an answer before it gives up.
request.timeout.why: A server that never answers would otherwise keep you waiting.
request.timeout.example: 5000 waits five seconds. 0 uses the default.
request.timeout.next: Raise it for slow operations such as large uploads.

table.enabled.title: Use this row
table.enabled.what: Turns the row on or off without deleting it.
table.enabled.why: You can try a request with and without a value quickly.
table.enabled.example: Clear the box to leave page=2 out for one send.
table.enabled.next: The cross at the end of the row deletes it.

response.status.title: Status, time, and size
response.status.what: The server's verdict, how long it took, and how big the answer was.
response.status.why: The status tells at a glance whether the request worked.
response.status.example: 200 OK worked, 404 not found, 401 not allowed, 500 the server failed.
response.status.next: The guide explains the codes you will meet most.

response.tabs.title: Body and Headers of the answer
response.tabs.what: Body shows the content of the answer, Headers the information about it.
response.tabs.why: Most of the time you need the body; headers help when something is unclear.
response.tabs.example: Content-Type in Headers says what kind of content came back.

response.pretty.title: Pretty and Raw
response.pretty.what: Pretty indents JSON and XML so they are easy to read; Raw shows the text exactly as it came.
response.pretty.why: Pretty is easier to read, Raw shows what the server really sent.
response.pretty.example: A long one-line JSON becomes an indented tree with line numbers.
response.pretty.next: Copy the body from Raw if you need it unchanged.

response.body.title: Body of the answer
response.body.what: The content the server sent back.
response.body.why: This is usually the data you asked for.
response.body.example: A list of users in JSON.
response.body.next: Select text and press Ctrl+C to copy it.

response.headers.title: Headers of the answer
response.headers.what: Information the server sent about its answer.
response.headers.why: They tell the format, caching, cookies, and more.
response.headers.next: Most of the time you can ignore them.

environments.list.title: Environments
environments.list.what: Your sets of variables, for example one per server.
environments.list.why: Switching the environment switches all values at once.
environments.list.next: Select one to edit its variables on the right.

environments.add.title: Add environment
environments.add.example: Add "Staging" and give it its own baseUrl.
environments.add.next: Type its name, then add variables.

environments.duplicate.title: Duplicate environment
environments.duplicate.what: Copies the selected environment with all its variables.
environments.duplicate.why: Faster than typing the same variables again.
environments.duplicate.example: Copy "Staging" to start "Production", then change the values.

environments.remove.title: Remove environment
environments.remove.what: Deletes the selected environment and its variables.
environments.remove.why: To get rid of one you no longer need.
environments.remove.next: Requests that used its variables show them as unresolved.

environments.name.title: Environment name
environments.name.what: The name shown in the selector at the top.
environments.name.why: A clear name avoids sending to the wrong server.
environments.name.next: It is stored when you leave the field.

environments.variables.title: Variables
environments.variables.what: Names with values that requests can use as {{name}}.
environments.variables.why: Write a value once and use it in many requests.
environments.variables.next: Tick Secret for passwords and keys: the value stays out of the workspace file.

curl.input.title: cURL command
curl.input.what: Paste a curl command here to turn it into a request.
curl.input.why: API documentation and browsers often give requests as curl commands.
curl.input.example: In a browser: Developer tools > Network > right-click > Copy as cURL (bash).
curl.input.next: The line below tells what was understood; press Import.

curl.import.title: Import
curl.import.what: Adds the request from the command to your collection and opens it.
curl.import.why: You can then edit and send it like any other.
curl.import.example: Options ReqDeck cannot use are listed before you import.
curl.import.next: Check the URL and headers, then press Send.

launcher.open.title: Open workspace
launcher.open.what: Opens a workspace file from your disk.
launcher.open.why: A workspace holds your requests and environments.
launcher.open.next: Recent workspaces are listed above for one click.

launcher.create.title: Create workspace
launcher.create.what: Starts a new, empty workspace file.
launcher.create.why: Use one workspace per project or API.
launcher.create.next: Then add a request with Ctrl+N.

launcher.samples.title: Open samples
launcher.samples.what: Opens ready requests against free test services.
launcher.samples.why: The fastest way to see how ReqDeck works.
launcher.samples.example: Pick a request and press Send.
launcher.samples.next: The samples open at Get a post, ready to send: press Send.

launcher.recent.title: Recent workspaces
launcher.recent.example: The cross removes an entry from the list, not the file.
launcher.recent.next: Click a row to open it.

dialog.settings.title: Settings
dialog.settings.what: Language, folder for new workspaces, and update checks.
dialog.settings.why: To adapt ReqDeck to how you work.
dialog.settings.example: Turn off automatic update checks if you prefer to check yourself.
dialog.settings.next: Close the window when done; changes apply at once.

dialog.about.title: About ReqDeck
dialog.about.what: Version, license, and the parts ReqDeck is built from.
dialog.about.why: Useful when you report a problem.
dialog.about.example: Copy the version when you write to support.
dialog.about.next: ReqDeck is free software under the GPL.

dialog.update.title: Updates
dialog.update.what: Tells whether a newer ReqDeck exists and installs it.
dialog.update.why: New versions fix problems and add features.
dialog.update.example: Install the update when it suits you.
dialog.update.next: Your workspaces are not changed by an update.

dialog.workspace.title: Workspace
dialog.workspace.what: Name and folder of a new workspace.
dialog.workspace.why: The workspace is one file in that folder.

dialog.confirm.title: Confirmation
dialog.confirm.what: ReqDeck asks before it does something that cannot be undone.
dialog.confirm.why: So that nothing is lost by a slip of the mouse.
dialog.confirm.example: Unsaved changes: Save keeps them, Discard drops them, Cancel goes back.

log.panel.title: Log
log.panel.what: Messages of the application: what it did and what went wrong.
log.panel.example: Filter by level to see only warnings and errors.
log.panel.next: View > Hide Log Panel closes it.

help.panel.title: Help
help.panel.what: A short explanation of what you pointed at or were working in.
help.panel.why: So you can go on without searching a manual.
help.panel.example: Point at the URL field and press F1.
help.panel.next: Press F1 again or Escape to close it. More in the guide opens the PDF.

notification.title: Message
notification.what: A message about something that just happened, such as a warning.
notification.why: Some results need your attention, for example a file that could not be saved.
notification.next: Close it with the cross; the log keeps all messages.

launcher.language.title: Language
launcher.language.what: The language of menus, buttons, and messages.
launcher.language.why: Use ReqDeck in the language you read best.
launcher.language.next: The change applies at once; Settings in the main window offers the same choice.

response.tlsBanner.title: Untrusted certificate
response.tlsBanner.what: The server proves who it is with a certificate, and this one is not trusted by Windows.
response.tlsBanner.why: A wrong certificate can mean someone is pretending to be the server, so ReqDeck stops.
response.tlsBanner.example: A test server on your own computer often has a certificate made by itself.
response.tlsBanner.next: Press Continue only if you know the server. Otherwise ask its owner.

response.tlsContinue.title: Continue without the check
response.tlsContinue.what: Sends this request once more and skips the certificate check for this server only.
response.tlsContinue.why: Test servers often use certificates nobody signed, and you still need to try them.
response.tlsContinue.next: The answer shows a warning, and the log records it. The next request is checked again.

response.save.title: Save the response
response.save.what: Writes the answer to a file as it was received, without the Pretty formatting. A compressed answer is saved unpacked.
response.save.why: To keep a download, open the answer in another program, or get all of a very large one.
response.save.next: Choose where to save; a message says where the file went.

response.find.title: Find in the response
response.find.what: Looks for text in the answer and marks each place it occurs. Capital and small letters count as the same.
response.find.why: A long answer is easier to read when you jump to the part you need.
response.find.example: Type "email" to see every email field in a list of users.
response.find.next: Enter or F3 goes to the next match, Shift+Enter or Shift+F3 to the previous one, Esc closes.

dialog.restoreCopy.title: Restore previous copy
dialog.restoreCopy.what: Puts the workspace file and its secret values back as they were before ReqDeck changed their file format.
dialog.restoreCopy.why: If something looks wrong after an update, you get your data back as it was.
dialog.restoreCopy.example: File > Restore Previous Copy… after secrets were moved to the encrypted format.
dialog.restoreCopy.next: Choose Yes to restore. Changes made since the copy, saved or not, are lost.

request.moveToSecret.title: Move to a secret
request.moveToSecret.what: Moves the password, token, or key you typed into a secret variable of the active environment and puts {{name}} in the field.
request.moveToSecret.why: Text typed into a request is saved in the workspace file, which you may share. Secret values stay encrypted on this computer.
request.moveToSecret.example: A token abc123 becomes the secret variable token, and the field shows {{token}}.
request.moveToSecret.next: Save the workspace. Without an active environment, ReqDeck makes one named Default.

completer.title: Variable suggestions
completer.what: After you type {{, ReqDeck lists the variables of the active environment that start with what follows.
completer.why: You do not have to remember or spell variable names.
completer.next: Arrow keys choose, Enter or Tab inserts, Escape closes the list.

history.search.title: Search history
history.search.what: Shows only the entries that contain every word you type, in the method, address, status, or error.
history.search.why: To find an earlier request among many.
history.search.example: post orders finds POST requests to an address with orders.
history.search.next: Press the Down arrow to move into the list, then Enter to make a request of the entry.

dialog.missingValues.title: Values needed
dialog.missingValues.what: Before sending, ReqDeck asks for variables the request uses but the active environment does not have.
dialog.missingValues.why: So no request leaves with a literal {{name}} in it.
dialog.missingValues.example: {{token}} has no value: type it once and press OK.
dialog.missingValues.next: Tick Keep to save the values in the active environment; otherwise they count for this send only.

palette.title: Find a request or command
palette.what: Ctrl+K opens a search over all requests, by name and address, and the menu commands.
palette.why: To get anywhere without the mouse or the tree.
palette.example: list orders finds the request List orders.
palette.next: Arrows choose, Enter opens or runs, Escape closes.

dialog.folderSettings.title: Folder settings
dialog.folderSettings.what: Authorization and variables that the requests of a folder share.
dialog.folderSettings.why: Set a token once for a whole API instead of in every request; imported Postman collections need this.
dialog.folderSettings.example: A folder with Bearer {{token}}; its requests set to Inherit from folder send that token.
dialog.folderSettings.next: Right-click a folder > Folder Settings…. Inherit from parent folder passes the question up; No authentication stops it.

dialog.import.title: Import a collection
dialog.import.what: Brings a Postman collection or environment into this workspace.
dialog.import.why: To carry on with the requests you made in Postman.
dialog.import.example: Export a collection in Postman (Collection v2.1) and choose the file here.
dialog.import.next: Read what will not carry over, then press Import. The collection becomes a new folder; save the workspace to keep it.

chapters.title: Your first request in five minutes

blocks.text: A request is a message your computer sends to a server. The server answers with a response. That is all an API is: a server that answers requests from programs instead of from people with a browser.

items: Start ReqDeck and choose Open Samples.
ReqDeck opens the request "Get a post" from the folder JSONPlaceholder in the Collection on the left.
Look at the address in the middle: this is where the request goes.
On the right you see the answer: a green 200 OK and the post as JSON.

blocks.caption: A request in the middle, its answer on the right.

blocks.text: Not sure what something is? Point at it and press F1.

blocks.caption: Press F1 and ReqDeck explains what is under the pointer.

chapters.title: What a request is made of

blocks.text: Think of a request as a letter. The method is what you ask for, the address is where it goes, parameters and headers are notes on the envelope, and the body is the letter inside.

rows: Create something new. Usually with a body.

blocks.text: Parameters are added to the address after a question mark, for example ?page=2. Headers carry information about the request, such as the format you accept. The body carries data, most often as JSON.

blocks.caption: A JSON body for a POST request.

blocks.text: Ctrl+K finds any request by a few words of its name or address, and any menu command. In the tree, Ctrl+click or Shift+click selects several items, F2 renames, Delete deletes, and right-click > Sort A–Z orders a folder.
A variable is a name for a value you use in many requests. Write {{baseUrl}} instead of the full server address, and change the address in one place.
An environment is a set of variables. Make one for each server, for example Staging and Production, and switch between them at the top of the window.
A {{name}} in red with an underline has no value in the active environment.
Tick Secret for passwords and keys. Their values are then kept out of the workspace file.
A field that names a variable the active environment does not have gets a red frame. Point at the field to see which variable is missing.
Type {{ and ReqDeck lists the variables of the active environment; Enter inserts one. If a request uses a variable the environment lacks, Send asks for its value first.
Many APIs answer only to users they know. The Auth tab adds the proof to each request.

rows: A token the service gave you.
A key, sent as a header or a parameter.

blocks.text: Use variables such as {{token}} with Secret ticked, so the value is not saved in the workspace file.

A password, token, or key you type into a request is saved in the workspace file. ReqDeck then offers Move to a secret: the value goes into a secret variable, encrypted on this computer, and the field shows {{token}} instead.
The first number tells whether the request worked. Codes starting with 2 mean success, with 4 a problem with the request, with 5 a problem on the server.

rows: It worked; there is nothing to show.
The server did not understand the request. Check the body and parameters.
You are not logged in, or the token expired.
You are logged in but not allowed.
Nothing at this address. Check the URL.
The server failed. Not your fault, usually.

blocks.caption: Status, time, size, and the body of the answer.

blocks.text: Ctrl+F finds text in the answer. The save button beside the size writes the answer to a file, also a very large one, of which only the start is shown.
Every request you send lands in History, on the left. Double-click an entry to make a new request from it. Passwords and tokens written in a request are not kept there.
Documentation often shows requests as curl commands. Use File > Import cURL to turn one into a request, and Request > Copy as cURL to share yours.

blocks.caption: History with the status of each request.

blocks.text: The search field above the history keeps the entries that contain every word you type, for example post orders.

Your requests live in the workspace file you chose, a .reqdeck file you may copy or share. Secret values of environments are not in it: ReqDeck keeps them encrypted for your Windows user on this computer.
On another computer, or under another Windows user, the secret values are empty. ReqDeck says so when the workspace opens. Enter them again and save.

Before a new version changes the format of these files, ReqDeck keeps a copy of the workspace file and its secret values. File > Restore Previous Copy puts them back; changes made since then are lost.
Two ReqDeck windows can run at once: both add to the same history.

rows: Nothing answers at this address. Is the server running? Is the port right?
The server name is wrong or the network is down.
The server took too long. Raise the timeout or try later.
A {{name}} has no value. Pick the right environment.
The server's HTTPS certificate is not trusted, common on test servers. If you know the server, press Continue.
ReqDeck uses the proxy set in Windows, like your browser. Requests to your own computer always go directly.
Secret values are empty on another computer
Secret values are encrypted for your Windows user on the computer where you saved them. On another computer or user, enter them again and save. The workspace file itself is not affected.

blocks.text: View > Show Log Panel shows what ReqDeck did and what went wrong.
